openers.mkt: In 1997 Costa Rica became the first country to run a national program that pays landowners for the services their land provides. This part of the course follows that idea: paying farmers and landowners to manage land so that it delivers clean water, stored carbon or thriving wildlife. China, the United States and the mineral-water brand Vittel have all tried versions of it, and Uganda tested one as a randomized controlled trial. Every scheme meets the same hard question. Did the payment cause an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a prediction of what would have happened without it?
openers.payments-for-ecosystem-services: A payment for ecosystem services offers farmers or landowners money to manage their land so that it keeps providing a service from nature. The US Conservation Reserve Program pays farmers to plant grass, trees or buffer strips on cropland. China's Grain for Green, launched in 1999, pays them to turn eroding farmland back into vegetation. This chapter looks at how such schemes are designed, from auctions in which sellers underbid one another to the rule that money flows only when the service is delivered. It also asks how anyone can tell whether a payment made a difference at all.

nature-mkt-136.title: Paying landowners for the services their land provides
nature-mkt-136.text: Climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation draw most of the money. They are the 'big three' of payment for ecosystem services, or PES. The idea is simple: farmers or landowners are paid to manage their land so that it keeps providing an ecosystem service. One definition calls PES a transparent system for securing additional environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers. The provider usually holds the property rights over the land and is compensated by those who benefit from its services. For a deal to make sense to both sides, beneficiaries should pay less than the service is worth to them. Providers, in turn, should accept more than it costs them to supply it. In practice, few deals are direct contracts between a buyer and a seller. Most programs are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, groups that sit outside government. PES is often promoted as a tool for rural development, though most programs are not designed mainly to reduce poverty. National programs that pay farmers to set land aside exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland, as well as the US and China.

nature-mkt-144.title: Additionality: would it have happened anyway?
nature-mkt-144.text: Paying someone to do what they were going to do anyway buys nothing. Additionality is the test for that trap. It asks whether an intervention, such as a payment or a credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened otherwise. The answer depends on a baseline, a prediction of what people would do without the policy, with everything else held constant. Strictly, additionality is the intervention's impact minus the impact of that reference case. It must also be counted net of side effects such as deadweight, paying for what would happen anyway, and leakage, harm pushed somewhere else. Displacement and substitution can shrink the gain in similar ways. A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway. That scenario is called business as usual. Additionality can be checked after the fact, as in program evaluation, or beforehand, as a screen for which projects may issue environmental credits. The stakes are high. Large markets for {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} have shown serious shortcomings on it. Problems with additionality and double counting can also undermine trust in the offsets described in {{ref:nature-mkt-081}}. One industry watchdog, the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market, cited additionality concerns when it excluded several renewable energy crediting methods. Every payment scheme in this chapter rises or falls on this question.

nature-mkt-145.title: Watershed management: sharing the water a landscape gathers
nature-mkt-145.text: One group's actions upstream can harm everyone downstream, and that is why watersheds need managing. A watershed is the land that drains into one river, lake or stream. Watershed management plans and runs programs that keep a watershed working and share its resources sustainably among its plants, animals and people. It covers water supply, water quality, drainage, stormwater runoff and water rights. On farms the tools include buffer strips, grassed waterways, restored wetlands, conservation tillage and crop rotation. In towns, retention ponds, filters and wetlands let stormwater soak in, so soil and plants clean it before it reaches streams. People are the hard part. Groups sharing a watershed often have unequal and divergent interests. Even the basic framing is disputed: donors backed by the World Bank argue freshwater should be priced as an economic good, while NGOs see it as a social good. States sharing the Rhine, Nile and Lake Chad basins have tried network governance, in which stakeholders form voluntary partnerships.

nature-mkt-141.title: The Conservation Reserve Program: paying US farmers not to plow
nature-mkt-141.text: More than 9 billion tons of soil had been kept from eroding by December 1, 2015, thanks to one American program. The Conservation Reserve Program, run by the US Department of Agriculture, pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips. It is a payment for ecosystem services on a national scale. Its aims are to reduce soil erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife. It grew out of the Soil Bank of the 1950s and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill, with contracts of 10 to 15 years. Farmers receive rental payments, up to 50% of the cost of establishing cover, and extra incentives. Money is limited, so only the most qualified land is enrolled. The benefits reach beyond the fields. In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving farmland. Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

nature-mkt-137.title: Three ways of seeing payments for nature
nature-mkt-137.text: Is paying a farmer to keep a forest a sensible trade, an imperfect tool, or a moral mistake? Thinkers give three broad answers, and they still disagree. Environmental economics sees a payment for ecosystem services as a voluntary, conditional deal between a buyer and a seller of a service, rooted in the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. Reality is messier than the theory. Transaction costs, the costs of making and policing a deal, are almost always present. Promises of future payments are not time consistent, meaning a payer may later prefer to break them. Financing often runs short. Ecological economics treats natural and manufactured capital as complements: one cannot simply stand in for the other. It judges a scheme by the weight of its incentive, how directly the money reaches providers, and how far the service is turned into a commodity. Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard. The third view rejects the idea of ecosystem services altogether. These critics argue that nature should be valued for its own sake, and that a market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people. Pragmatists accept the problems of putting a value on nature. Still, they argue, in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'. The split between the first two schools is traced in {{ref:nature-found-039}}.

nature-mkt-148.title: Reverse auctions: letting sellers bid the price down
nature-mkt-148.text: In an ordinary, or forward, auction, buyers bid prices up. A reverse auction flips the roles. One buyer faces many sellers, and the sellers compete by underbidding each other, so prices typically fall. Government procurement through public tenders is a common example. For conservation the format has a special use. A landowner knows the {{ref:nature-econ-095}} of setting land aside, while the program paying for it does not. Bids in a reverse auction reveal those private costs, which helps design incentive programs for public goods, shared resources and ecosystem services. Each seller should first work out the lowest price it will accept, which requires knowing its true marginal cost, the cost of supplying one more unit. In a scoring auction, the buyer announces in advance how it will score the price and other features of each offer.

nature-mkt-143.title: Grain for Green: China trades fields for forest
nature-mkt-143.text: Some 124 million people in 1,897 counties across 25 provinces have taken part in Grain for Green. China launched the program in 1999 to pay farmers for turning erosion-prone farmland back into vegetation, curbing flooding and soil erosion. It is a payment for ecosystem services in a very literal form: farmers receive grain for not farming forested slopes. By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation. The bill is large and uncertain. One account puts the cost at $43 billion, while some sources cite $95 billion for the whole program. On the whole it has paid off economically and reduced erosion and flooding. Its weak spot is wildlife. Many plantings were cheap single-species stands that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.

nature-mkt-138.title: Costa Rica's pioneering national payment scheme
nature-mkt-138.text: In 1997 Costa Rica set up Pagos por servicios ambientales, the first program of payments for ecosystem services run on a national scale. It pays for four services: greenhouse gas mitigation, water services, biodiversity protection and scenic beauty. A fuel tax paid for it at first, and a water tariff was added in 2006. By the end of 2005 its contracts covered 10% of the country. It is estimated to have prevented 11 million tons of carbon emissions from 1999 to 2005. Its flat payment has a flaw. Many high-value areas stay out, because their opportunity costs are higher than the payment.

nature-mkt-140.title: Uganda's forest payment experiment
nature-mkt-140.text: Between 2010 and 2013, forest owners in Hoima and Kibaale, Uganda, took part in the first payment scheme set up as a {{ref:nature-econ-254}} to measure its effect on deforestation. Owners were paid $28 per hectare per year for two years to keep their forest intact, about 5% of typical annual income. Deforestation ran at 2 to 5% in participating villages, against 7 to 10% in control villages. The scheme ended once the evaluation was done. Old forest practices are assumed to resume once payments stop.

nature-mkt-139.title: Vittel pays farmers to protect its spring water
nature-mkt-139.text: From the 1970s, more intensive farming raised nitrate levels in the aquifer, the underground water store, behind Vittel mineral water. The brand itself was under threat. The pollution came from many scattered sources, so no single farmer's share could be measured. The company negotiated instead. It bought some land and gave nearby farmers technical support and time-limited payments to change their practices. The deal is perhaps the world's best-known payment for ecosystem services built on direct negotiation. It is often cited as a case of the private bargaining described by the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. Community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

nature-mkt-150.title: Baselines: measuring against a world that never happened
nature-mkt-150.text: Knowing what a payment achieved means knowing what would have happened without it, and that world can never be observed. The baseline, or counterfactual, is that predicted outcome without the payment or project, against which its real effect is measured. Establishing it is a key challenge for any claim that payments for ecosystem services work. Carbon markets show why. Under the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}, credits are issued for the monitored gap between baseline and actual emissions. Because the baseline cannot be seen, it is built from hypothetical scenarios, similar activities elsewhere, or emissions before the project. That invites gaming. Project partners may gain from a high baseline, risking spurious credits, and offsets can even reward emitting more to inflate it. How much leakage gets counted also depends partly on how the baseline is drawn. It is the hidden half of every judgment about additionality.

nature-mkt-149.title: No service, no payment: the rule of conditionality
nature-mkt-149.text: No service, no money. Conditionality is the rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up. It sits inside one well-known definition of PES: additional environmental services secured through conditional payments to voluntary providers. Most design debates turn on how conditions are set and enforced through monitoring and verification. The idea also runs through social policy. The programs described in {{ref:nature-mkt-146}} pay families for schooling and health care, and in Mexico the conditions raised secondary-school attendance most. Conditions are not welcome everywhere. Supporters of a rights-based approach to development argue strongly against attaching them to social cash transfers.

nature-mkt-152.title: Paying for results, not promises
nature-mkt-152.text: Most payment programs pay for management practices, and only less commonly for measured outcomes. Results-based payments reverse that. Money flows only for measured, verified environmental results, such as emission reductions, rather than for planned actions. Forests are the biggest test. {{ref:nature-mkt-092}} uses such payments to put a financial value on carbon stored in forests, as the last of four stages after readiness, a finance agreement and verification. To qualify, a country needs a national system for monitoring its forests, documented methods and data, and reporting under the Warsaw Framework. It also needs an assessed benchmark of its past forest emissions and a report on how agreed social and environmental safeguards are respected. The Carbon Fund of the {{ref:nature-mkt-101}} pays only after independent verification of reported cuts. The Green Climate Fund ran a pilot from 2017 to 2022 and made it a permanent window in 2024. Farming has a version too. The European Commission defines results-based schemes as paying for outcomes such as breeding birds, leaving the methods to the farmer.

nature-mkt-147.title: How New York City keeps its water clean by guarding its watersheds
nature-mkt-147.text: Only 10% of New York City's water is filtered, though all of it is disinfected. The rest stays clean because the city protects the upstate watersheds that supply it. Its three systems, Croton, Catskill and Delaware, reach up to 125 miles (201 km) north of the city. Together they deliver over 1.2 billion US gallons a day to more than eight million residents. Since 1997 the city has bought, or protected through legal limits on development, over 130,000 acres (53,000 ha) of watershed land. The Department of Environmental Protection runs a $1.5 billion Watershed Protection Program. The payoff is a partial exemption from filtration rules. That spares the city more than $10 billion for a filtration plant and at least $100 million a year to run it. In 2018 the city announced a further US$1 billion investment to keep its unfiltered supply pure, partly against cloudier water driven by climate change. Here a protected landscape does the work of a machine.

nature-mkt-146.title: Conditional cash transfers: paying families to choose school
nature-mkt-146.text: Few development programs have been evaluated as rigorously as conditional cash transfers. These programs fight poverty by paying cash only to people who meet conditions, such as sending children to school or getting them vaccinated. By 2011 they had spread to 18 Latin American countries, covering up to 129 million people. Brazil's Bolsa Família, for example, pays poor households if school-age children are enrolled and younger children vaccinated. The conditions seem to matter. Evidence from Mexico and Malawi found they raised school enrollment compared with unconditional payments.

nature-mkt-151.title: Putting conservation money where it counts most
nature-mkt-151.text: A flat payment treats every hectare alike, but land is not alike. Spatial targeting means directing conservation payments to the places where they buy the most environmental benefit for the money. Costa Rica shows the cost of skipping it. Its flat-rate payments leave many high-value areas unenrolled, because landowners there face higher opportunity costs. Its water tariff, tied to particular watersheds, was criticized for concentrating money in areas of relatively low ecological importance. Two tools help. Reverse auctions can reveal what each landowner really needs to be paid. The Conservation Reserve Program, with limited money, admits only the most qualified land.

nature-mkt-142.title: Farm stewardship schemes in England and Switzerland
nature-mkt-142.text: An environmental management scheme gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment. England runs such schemes under Environmental Stewardship, administered by Natural England. After leaving the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, the British government started its Environmental Land Management scheme in 2024. Switzerland ties the money directly to practice. Since 1998 it has made farm subsidies depend on good environmental care, such as keeping at least 7% of farmland as ecological compensation areas.

reviews.payments-for-ecosystem-services: Every scheme in this chapter shares one design: pay landowners to manage land for services others enjoy, and pay only when the service is delivered. The examples run from national programs in Costa Rica, the United States and China to Vittel's private deal with nearby farmers. New York City shows the logic most sharply, guarding upstate watersheds instead of spending more than $10 billion on a filtration plant. Design decides how much nature each dollar buys: reverse auctions reveal landowners' costs, while flat rates leave high-value land unenrolled. Underneath it all sits additionality, judged against a baseline no one can observe, which is why Uganda's randomized trial stands out.
